evidence.title: Coherence and indistinguishability of highly pure single photons from non-resonantly and resonantly excited telecom C-band quantum dots
evidence.text: However, especially regarding quantum communication schemes, an emission wavelength around 1550 nm (Telecom C-band) is much soughtafter both for satellite-based quantum communication due to an atmospheric transmission window and the possibility to perform it in broad daylight 8 , as well as for its fiber-based counterpart due to the global absorption minimum and low dispersion of standard glass fibers forming the existing global fiber network 9 .However, to extend the range of quantum communication applications such as quantum key distribution 10,11 , quantum relays 12,13 or quantum repeaters [14][15][16][17] are needed.The ideal light source for such applications combines bright single-photon and entangled-photon pair emission with a high degree of indistinguishability at 1550 nm. The emission of single and entangled photons in the telecom C-band has been demonstrated in two material systems, namely InAs/InP 18,19 and InAs/InGaAs/GaAs 20,21 .The last requirement, i.e. the indistinguishability of photons, is of major importance because it is necessary for two-photon interference (TPI), enabling linear-optic Bell state measurements and, therefore, entanglement swapping 22,23 in quantum repeater schemes.An experimental demonstration at this wavelength has been elusive in both material systems up to now.a) Electronic mail: c.nawrath@ihfg.uni-stuttgart.de;www.ihfg.uni-stuttgart.deHowever, long coherence times and the teleportation of a quantum state have been demonstrated in the InAs/InP system 24 , promising a high degree of indistinguishability.For QDs based on GaAs on the other hand, a straightforeward implementation of distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) offers the prospect of fabricating high-quality cavities and micropillars with a high extraction efficiency [1][2][3]25 . Furhermore, the recently demonstrated feasibility of strain-tuning 26 paves the way to tune different QDs into resonance, facilitating remote TPI experiments 27,28 .

strategy_plan.planning_summary: This is a dichroic filter design problem: high transmittance at 1530-1565 nm (quantum signal) with high reflectance at 400-700 nm (solar background rejection). The literature provides strong support for HfO2/SiO2 as a material pair (L04, L07, L16, L25, L28, L34, L40) and the cold mirror concept (L33) directly matches this spectral requirement. Four genuinely distinct strategy axes are proposed: (1) periodic Bragg stack testing classic cold mirror design, (2) aperiodic thickness-optimized stack testing whether breaking periodicity improves band-edge sharpness, (3) AR-matched Bragg stack testing whether impedance matching reduces passband ripple, and (4) chirped Bragg stack testing whether thickness grading broadens the reflection band. Each route has one fixed topology and one distinct design variable, ensuring comparable iteration results.

routes.design_principle: Quarter-wave optical thickness (QWOT) stacks create constructive interference for reflection at design wavelengths. For a dichroic filter blocking 400-700nm while passing 1530-1565nm, the high-index HfO2 and low-index SiO2 layers should have optical thicknesses near λ/4 at a center wavelength in the visible blocking band. However, pure QWOT initialization creates symmetry that can trap gradient-based optimizers; harmonic perturbations (λ/8, λ/2 multiples) break this symmetry while remaining physically meaningful.
